message:
QUESTION: Which of the three tariffs (Fixed, Variable or Time-of-use) will give the household the lowest total energy bill over the next 12 months, and by how much? DATA: A household is choosing an energy tariff for the next 12 months (365 days). It is currently on the Variable tariff and can switch freely: none of the tariffs below has an exit fee. Last 12 months' usage: electricity 3,100 kWh, gas 12,000 kWh. About 15% of the household's current electricity use falls in the off-peak window (dishwasher and washing machine on timers). The household takes delivery of an electric car next week. It expects to need about 2,400 kWh a year of home charging, all of which it will schedule in the off-peak window. Gas use is not expected to change. | Tariff | Electricity unit rate | Electricity standing charge | Gas unit rate | Gas standing charge | | Fixed (F) | 24.5p/kWh | 55p/day | 6.2p/kWh | 30p/day | | Variable (V) | 22.0p/kWh | 60p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day | | Time-of-use (E) | 30.0p/kWh peak; 8.0p/kWh off-peak (00:30-05:30) | 50p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day | Rates on V can change at the supplier's discretion with 30 days' notice; the supplier has announced no change. F and E are fixed for 12 months. Ignore VAT (rates already include it). KNOWN FLAWS: F1. [calculation] 3,100 × £0.245 = £759.50, not £734.50. CORRECTION: F electricity £960.25; F total £1,813.75 (with no exit fee). F2. [misreport] The data state that none of the tariffs has an exit fee. CORRECTION: No exit fees apply. F costs £1,813.75 on last year's usage. F3. [method] Uses an unweighted average of peak and off-peak rates instead of weighting by the household's usage (15% off-peak). CORRECTION: On last year's usage: 2,635 kWh × 30p + 465 kWh × 8p = £827.70, plus £182.50 = £1,010.20; E total £1,843.35. Without the car, E is the most expensive and V (£1,734.15) is cheapest. F4. [omission] Ignores the electric car arriving next week, which adds about 2,400 kWh of off-peak charging over the year being priced. CORRECTION: With the car: F £1,813.75 + 2,400 × 24.5p = £2,401.75; V £1,734.15 + 2,400 × 22p = £2,262.15; E £1,843.35 + 2,400 × 8p = £2,035.35. E is cheapest, saving £226.80 a year against V (for the right reason). EXTENSIONS: - Break-even analysis: on base usage alone, E beats V on electricity only if the off-peak share exceeds about 31% (E electricity = £1,112.50 − £682 × share, vs V £901). With 2,400 kWh of car charging the off-peak share rises to (465 + 2,400) / 5,500, about 52%, well above break-even. - Sensitivity to car mileage: E stays cheaper than V as long as off-peak car charging exceeds about 780 kWh a year (the £109.20 E-V gap on base usage divided by the 14p/kWh rate advantage). - Price risk on V: show the bill if V rises by, say, 10% from month 4, to quantify the value of E's 12-month fix. FINAL VERSION: # Energy Tariff Comparison for the Next 12 Months ## Answer **Time-of-use (E) gives the lowest bill: £2,035.35 for the year.** - That is **£226.80 less than staying on Variable (V)**, which costs £2,262.15. V is the second-cheapest tariff. - It is **£366.40 less than Fixed (F)**, which costs £2,401.75. The car arrives next week, so it will charge for about 51 of the 52 weeks. That trims the realistic saving against V to **about £220**. The ranking stays the same. ## Usage for the next 12 months | | Peak | Off-peak | Total | |---|---|---|---| | Existing use (3,100 kWh, 15% off-peak) | 2,635 | 465 | 3,100 | | Car charging (all off-peak) | 0 | 2,400 | 2,400 | | **Total electricity** | **2,635** | **2,865** | **5,500** | | Gas (unchanged) | | | 12,000 | ## Costs (365 days) | | Fixed (F) | Variable (V) | Time-of-use (E) | |---|---|---|---| | Electricity units | 5,500 × 24.5p = £1,347.50 | 5,500 × 22.0p = £1,210.00 | 2,635 × 30p = £790.50
2,865 × 8p = £229.20 | | Electricity standing charge | 55p × 365 = £200.75 | 60p × 365 = £219.00 | 50p × 365 = £182.50 | | **Electricity total** | **£1,548.25** | **£1,429.00** | **£1,202.20** | | Gas units | 12,000 × 6.2p = £744.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | | Gas standing charge | 30p × 365 = £109.50 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | | **Gas total** | **£853.50** | **£833.15** | **£833.15** | | **Annual total** | **£2,401.75** | **£2,262.15** | **£2,035.35** | | **Extra cost compared with E** | **+£366.40** | **+£226.80** | n/a | ## Why E wins - **Gas costs the same on V and E**, so all of E's advantage comes from electricity. - **The car is what makes E cheapest.** - On last year's usage alone, E would cost **£109.20 more** than V (£1,010.20 against £901.00). - That is because 85% of existing use is at peak, where E charges 30p and V charges 22p. - **Off-peak charging is much cheaper on E.** - Each kWh charged off-peak costs 8p on E and 22p on V, a saving of 14p. - Over 2,400 kWh that saves £336. - The £336 covers the £109.20 penalty and leaves **£226.80**. - **F is dearer than V at this household's usage.** - F's higher unit rates add £161.50 (£137.50 on electricity, £24.00 on gas). - F's lower standing charges save £21.90. - Net, F costs **£139.60 more** than V. F would only beat V for a household using very little energy. ## How robust is the result? | Risk | E stays cheapest as long as… | Likelihood | |---|---|---| | Less car charging than expected | Off-peak car charging is at least **780 kWh** (£109.20 ÷ 14p), about a third of the estimate. | Low | | Some charging happens at peak | No more than about **1,030 kWh (43%)** of charging lands at peak. Each kWh moved to peak adds 22p to E's bill and nothing to V's. | Low, if charging is scheduled | | V's rates are cut | V's cuts save less than about **£227** over the year. Electricity alone would need to fall below about **17.9p** for the full year. Allowing for the 30 days' notice, it would need to fall to about **17.5p**. A gas-only cut would need to be about 1.9p or more. | Low. No change has been announced. A rise in V's rates only widens E's lead. | **F only becomes the best choice if two things go wrong at once:** - More than about **1,665 kWh (about 70%)** of charging lands at peak, so F beats E. - V's rates also rise enough to make V dearer than F. For electricity alone, that means a rise of about **2.5p** for the full year, or about **2.8p** if it starts after the notice period. **None of these risks locks the household in.** No tariff has an exit fee, so if any of them materialises the household can switch at no cost. **There is upside too.** Each extra kWh of existing use moved into the off-peak window saves a further 22p on E. A tumble dryer on a timer is one example. **The off-peak window is long enough.** 2,400 kWh a year averages about 6.6 kWh a night. - A 7 kW charger delivers that in about an hour. - A 3-pin plug at about 2.3 kW delivers about 11.5 kWh in the 5-hour window. That covers the average night, but a very flat battery may need two nights. ## Recommendation **Switch to Time-of-use (E).** It saves about £220 over the year against staying on V and about £360 against F. It also fixes prices for 12 months, which V does not. To get the saving, the household should: 1. **Check the meter.** E needs a smart meter that records peak and off-peak use separately. 2. **Confirm the off-peak hours with the supplier.** Some meters keep the window in GMT, which means 01:30–06:30 during British Summer Time. Set the car and appliance timers to match. 3. **Set the car to charge only in the off-peak window.** Also turn off any app features that top up or pre-heat the car outside the window. Keep the dishwasher and washing machine timers as they are. 4. **Check that charging is landing off-peak, using two simple tests.** - **Charger or car app log.** Most chargers and cars record when each session ran. Any regular charging outside 00:30–05:30 needs fixing. - **Off-peak share on each bill.** Divide off-peak kWh by total kWh. As planned, the share should be about **50% or more**. - About **43%** means roughly a fifth of charging is at peak. Fix the scheduling. - About **33%** means the saving over V has gone. If the scheduling cannot be fixed, switch back to V. The share works without any history from last year, and it is fairly stable across seasons. (Leave out the first bill, which covers the week before the car arrives.) --- ### What changed in this review - **Re-verified every figure.** The totals, the differences, all thresholds (780, 1,030 and 1,665 kWh; 17.9p, 17.5p, 2.5p and 2.8p) and the roughly £220 part-year saving are all correct. - **Replaced the bill-check trigger.** The old check compared monthly peak kWh with "the same month last year". - That needs last year's peak/off-peak split month by month. A household on a single-rate tariff may not have it. - The 40 kWh signal is also small against normal month-to-month swings of about 220 kWh. - The new check uses the charger log and the off-peak share, which need no history. - **Broadened the V-cut threshold.** It is now stated as a £227 annual saving from any rate change, with an electricity figure and a gas figure. The old draft only covered electricity and explained why in a confusing way. A gas cut on V does erode E's lead. - **Removed duplication and tightened the wording.** The conclusions are unchanged.
